```{r setup}
library(multisiteDGP)
```

multisiteDGP simulates the summary data of a multisite trial from a two-stage
model: a distribution for the site effects, and a normal distribution for the
estimate of each site around its site effect. The sections below state the
model, show the function that carries out each of the four steps of a
simulation, and map the symbols to the arguments.

## The two-stage model

A trial has $J$ sites. Site $j$ has a site effect $\tau_j$, an estimate
$\hat\tau_j$ of it, and the standard error $\mathrm{se}_j$ of the estimate.
The observation stage is the distribution of the estimate given the other
two.

$$
\hat\tau_j \mid \tau_j, \mathrm{se}_j \sim N(\tau_j, \mathrm{se}_j^2)
$$

The second argument of $N$ is a variance. The estimates of different sites
are independent, and the standard errors are treated as known. The
site-effect stage is the distribution of the site effects.

$$
\tau_j = \tau + \mathbf{x}_j^\top \boldsymbol\beta + \sigma_\tau z_j
$$

The grand mean is $\tau$ and the cross-site standard deviation is
$\sigma_\tau$. The standardized site effects $z_j$ are independent draws from
a distribution $G$ with mean 0 and variance 1, normal by default. The term
$\mathbf{x}_j^\top \boldsymbol\beta$ is a linear function of site covariates
and is absent by default. With it, $\sigma_\tau$ is the standard deviation of
the site effects around $\tau + \mathbf{x}_j^\top \boldsymbol\beta$.

Lee et al. [-@lee2025improving] use these two stages for multisite trials.
With normal site effects and no covariates, they are the random-effects model
of meta-analysis. The model takes the standard errors as given. The package
also generates them, and can make them depend on the site effects.

## The four steps

`sim_multisite()` simulates from the model in four steps, and each step has a
function of its own that you can call. Each function takes the data frame
that the one before it returns.

```{r steps}
set.seed(1)
effects <- gen_effects(J = 10, tau = 0, sigma_tau = 0.2)
sizes <- gen_site_sizes(effects, J = 10, nj_mean = 50, cv = 0.5)
sizes
aligned <- align_rank_corr(sizes, rank_corr = 0.3)
by_hand <- gen_observations(aligned)
by_hand
```

In the first tibble, `gen_effects()` has created `site_index`, `z_j`, and
`tau_j`, and `gen_site_sizes()` has added `n_j`, `se2_j`, and `se_j`. In the
second, `align_rank_corr()` has reordered those three columns across sites and
`gen_observations()` has added `tau_j_hat`. `sim_multisite()` makes the same
four calls with the arguments in its design, whose defaults are the values
used above.

```{r same}
dat <- sim_multisite(J = 10, dependence = "rank", rank_corr = 0.3, seed = 1)
identical(dat$tau_j_hat, by_hand$tau_j_hat)
```

The seeded call returns the same estimates as the four calls.

### Site effects

`gen_effects()` carries out the site-effect stage. It draws $z_j$ from the
distribution named by `true_dist` and computes $\tau_j$. Site 1 has `z_j`
equal to $-0.626$, so its `tau_j` is $0.2 \times (-0.626) = -0.125$. The
built-in distributions are the normal, Student t, skew normal, asymmetric
Laplace, a mixture of two normals, and a point mass at zero with a slab, each
standardized to mean 0 and variance 1. `true_dist = "User"` takes the draws
from the function `g_fn`. The arguments `formula`, `data`, and `beta` supply
the covariate term, where $\mathbf{x}_j$ is row $j$ of the model matrix.

### Site sizes and standard errors

`gen_site_sizes()` draws a site size $n_j$ for each site and derives the
sampling variance from it.

$$
\mathrm{se}_j^2 = \frac{\kappa}{n_j}, \qquad
\kappa = \left( \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{1 - p} \right) (1 - R^2) \, \sigma_Y^2
$$

This is the variance of a difference in means between $p n_j$ treated and
$(1 - p) n_j$ control individuals, where $p$ is the proportion treated. The
outcome variance is $\sigma_Y^2$, and $R^2$ is the share of it that covariates
of the individuals explain. `compute_kappa()` returns $\kappa$, which is 4
with the defaults $p = 0.5$, $R^2 = 0$, and $\sigma_Y^2 = 1$. Site 1 in the
first tibble has 19 individuals, so its sampling variance is $4 / 19 = 0.211$
and its standard error is 0.459.

The site sizes are draws from a gamma distribution truncated below at
$n_{\min}$, with its two parameters chosen so that the truncated distribution
has mean $\bar n$ and coefficient of variation CV. Each draw is then rounded
down or up at random, which keeps the mean and adds a little variance.
`engine = "censored"` selects the procedure of Lee et al. (2025) instead,
which sets a gamma draw below $n_{\min}$ to $n_{\min}$.

`sim_meta()` sets the standard errors directly, with `gen_se_direct()` in
place of `gen_site_sizes()`. From a target informativeness $I$ and a
heterogeneity ratio $R$, it computes sampling variances that are evenly
spaced on the log scale and assigns them to the sites in random order.

$$
\mathrm{se}_j^2 = \mathrm{GM} \cdot R^{u_j - 1/2}, \qquad
\mathrm{GM} = \sigma_\tau^2 \, \frac{1 - I}{I}, \qquad
u_j = \frac{j - 1}{J - 1}
$$

Their geometric mean is GM and the largest is $R$ times the smallest.
Informativeness is $\sigma_\tau^2$ divided by the sum of $\sigma_\tau^2$ and
the geometric mean of the sampling variances, so it equals $I$ exactly. The
column `n_j` is `NA`.

### Dependence between effects and precision

The site sizes and standard errors are drawn independently of the site
effects. With `dependence = "none"`, the default, `sim_multisite()` skips this
step. Otherwise the step replaces $(n_j, \mathrm{se}_j)$ by
$(n_{\pi(j)}, \mathrm{se}_{\pi(j)})$ for a permutation $\pi$ of the sites. It
chooses $\pi$ so that the correlation between $z_j$ and $\mathrm{se}_j^2$ is
close to a target. A positive target pairs larger site effects with larger
standard errors. The set of standard errors does not change, only which site
has which, so $I$ and $R$ stay the same. Site 4 has the largest site effect.
It had 79 individuals before the step and has 19 after it, with the largest
standard error, 0.459.

`align_rank_corr()` swaps pairs of sites until the Spearman correlation is
within `tol` of `rank_corr`. `align_copula_corr()` orders the standard errors
by a normal score that has correlation `pearson_corr` with the normal scores
of the $z_j$. `align_hybrid_corr()` starts from the copula order and then
swaps pairs. `vignette("effect-precision-dependence")` compares the three.

### Observed estimates

`gen_observations()` carries out the observation stage. It draws
$\hat\tau_j = \tau_j + \mathrm{se}_j e_j$ with $e_j \sim N(0, 1)$,
independently for each site, and adds the result as `tau_j_hat`. Site 1 has a
site effect of $-0.125$ and, after the reordering, a standard error of 0.243.
Its estimate is 0.0976. A function supplied as `obs_fn` replaces the normal
draw.

## Notation and arguments

The arguments are those of `multisitedgp_design()`, and the columns are those
of the simulated data.

| Symbol | Meaning | Argument or column | Default |
|-----------------|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------|--------------|
| $J$ | number of sites | `J` | 50 |
| $\tau$ | grand mean | `tau` | 0 |
| $\sigma_\tau$ | cross-site standard deviation | `sigma_tau` | 0.2 |
| $G$ | distribution of $z_j$ | `true_dist`, `theta_G` | `"Gaussian"` |
| $\mathbf{x}_j$, $\boldsymbol\beta$ | site covariates and their coefficients | `formula`, `data`, `beta` | none |
| $z_j$, $\tau_j$ | standardized site effect and site effect | columns `z_j`, `tau_j` | |
| $\bar n$, CV, $n_{\min}$ | mean, coefficient of variation, and lower bound of the site sizes | `nj_mean`, `cv`, `nj_min` | 50, 0.5, 5 |
| $p$ | proportion treated | `p` | 0.5 |
| $R^2$ | share of outcome variance explained by covariates | `R2` | 0 |
| $\sigma_Y^2$ | outcome variance | `var_outcome` | 1 |
| $\kappa$ | sampling variance multiplied by site size | `compute_kappa()` | 4 |
| $I$ | informativeness | `I`, in `sim_meta()` only | none |
| $R$ | heterogeneity ratio, the largest $\mathrm{se}_j^2$ over the smallest | `R`, in `sim_meta()` only | 1 |
| $n_j$, $\mathrm{se}_j$, $\mathrm{se}_j^2$ | site size, standard error, and sampling variance | columns `n_j`, `se_j`, `se2_j` | |
| $\pi$ | reordering of the standard errors | `dependence`, `rank_corr`, `pearson_corr` | `"none"`, 0, 0 |
| $\hat\tau_j$ | observed estimate | column `tau_j_hat` | |

Lee et al. (2025) write the two stages in the same way, with $\sigma$ for the
cross-site standard deviation and $\widehat{se}_j$ for the standard error. The
hat is dropped here because a simulation sets the standard error and does not
estimate it. In the paper $G$ is the distribution of $\tau_j$, and here it is
its standardized form. `preset_jebs_strict()` returns a design from the
paper's simulation study. It has no covariates, no dependence, and
`engine = "censored"`.

## Assumptions and limits

- The estimate of a site is normal around its site effect. In very small
  sites this large-sample approximation can be poor.
- The standard errors are known. In a real trial they are estimates, and the
  model leaves out their sampling error.
- A design needs at least 10 sites and a positive `sigma_tau`, so a trial
  without cross-site variation cannot be simulated.
- Covariates enter only through $\mathbf{x}_j^\top \boldsymbol\beta$. They do
  not change $\sigma_\tau$ or the standard errors.
- Standard errors from site sizes assume one treatment and one control group
  per site, and the same $p$, $R^2$, and $\sigma_Y^2$ in every site.
  Cluster-randomized, blocked, and factorial designs are not covered.
- The dependence step sets a correlation by reordering. It does not model why
  site effects and site sizes would be related.
